analysis.one_liner: Repeals the rule requiring retirement advisers to put savers' interests first.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 34-26, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Labor Department's 2016 "fiduciary rule," which requires anyone giving retirement investment advice to act in the saver's best interest. In its place it sets a lighter standard for stockbrokers: recommendations must be in the customer's best interest "at the time they are made," but brokers can keep taking commissions from the products they sell, never have to recommend the cheapest option, and are not treated as fiduciaries under retirement law. It also blocks the Labor Department and Treasury from writing similar best-interest rules in the future and overrides any stronger state rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Broker-dealers and annuity sellers. The bill lets them keep the commission-based sales model — recommending products that pay them the most — without the legal duty, or lawsuit exposure, that comes with fiduciary status under retirement law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares the Labor Department's 2016 fiduciary rule and its related exemptions "shall have no force or effect," removing the requirement that retirement advisers act in the investor's best interest.

Under the replacement standard, simply receiving commissions or transaction-based compensation, recommending the broker's own or affiliated products, or recommending a limited menu of products would not by itself violate the standard of conduct.
The bill expressly says brokers are not required to recommend the least expensive security or strategy, and need not analyze all possible products before making a recommendation.
The bill creates new exemptions under ERISA and the tax code so broker recommendations and annuity sales governed by state insurance regulation can proceed without prohibited-transaction liability.

It bars the Secretary of Labor and the Secretary of the Treasury from promulgating any future rule defining fiduciary status that would impose obligations on brokers or insurers beyond the new Securities Exchange Act standard.

analysis.who_pays: People saving for retirement, who would keep paying commissions and sales charges on conflicted advice with a weaker legal remedy if the advice turned out to be self-serving. State regulators would also lose authority, since the new federal standard preempts state law on broker conduct.

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps the core conflict of interest in place: a broker can still be paid more to sell one product over another and is not required to recommend the cheapest option, so savers bear the cost of conflicted recommendations.

The bill preempts state law governing broker conduct and blocks future Labor Department and Treasury fiduciary rules, so states and the agency that wrote the original protection could not restore stronger standards.
The bill says complying with the new standard creates no presumption of fiduciary status under ERISA or other regimes, leaving savers with fewer legal tools than the fiduciary rule provided.

The strongest argument for the bill was that the Labor Department rule raised compliance costs and threatened small and middle-income savers' access to advice; but the bill addressed that by repealing the protection entirely and writing the broker industry's preferred standard into statute, rather than tailoring the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs almost entirely to broker-dealers and annuity sellers, who keep a sales model built on commissions and conflicts of interest; the cost falls on retirement savers, who keep paying those commissions without a true best-interest duty or the legal remedies that come with it. Even granting the concern that the Labor Department rule could limit advice for small accounts, this bill replaced the rule with a standard that expressly preserves paid product recommendations and shuts the door on future rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Financial Services Committee and was placed on the House calendar in late December 2018, but the Congress ended days later without the House ever voting on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 27, 2017 and referred to the Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees; a subcommittee had already held hearings on the topic that July.
The Financial Services Committee held markups in October 2017 and ordered the bill reported by a vote of 34 to 26.
The committee formally reported the bill on August 10, 2018, and the other two committees were twice granted extensions before being discharged on December 28, 2018.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 865 on December 28, 2018, but the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without the House ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirement savers came out ahead: the rule requiring advisers to act in their best interest was not repealed, and brokers and annuity sellers did not get the statutory protection they sought. They were better off simply because the bill ran out of time, not because it was defeated on the merits.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee's 34-26 vote to report the bill matched the panel's partisan split; the bill never reached a floor vote where any Democrats would have voted.

industries.note: The bill repeals the fiduciary rule that threatened their commission-based model and writes a replacement standard that explicitly permits commissions, proprietary products, and no duty to find the cheapest option. Savers would keep paying the higher costs those conflicts produce.

The bill creates new ERISA and tax-code exemptions so annuity sales can proceed under state insurance regulation alone, removing the fiduciary rule's restrictions on commission-heavy annuity sales to retirement savers.

The fiduciary rule would have pushed retirement savers toward advisers paid only by fees; repealing it removes that competitive advantage and keeps advisers competing against commission-based brokers. Their interest runs alongside savers' here.
